title: Operate and monitor a lathe to produce simple components

lessons.title: The lathe and lathe safety
lessons.html:
What a lathe does

A lathe is a machine that turns a workpiece while a cutting tool removes metal. In an agricultural equipment workshop, a centre lathe is used to make simple parts such as pins, bushes, spacers and shafts, to face the ends of bars, to drill centre holes and to turn down worn parts for repair.

Main parts of a centre lathe

PartFunction
BedThe strong base with slideways along which the carriage and tailstock move
HeadstockHolds the spindle and gearbox that turn the work
ChuckGrips the workpiece (three-jaw self-centring or four-jaw independent)
TailstockSupports long work with a centre, or holds drills
Carriage and saddleMoves the tool along the bed
Cross-slideMoves the tool in and out across the work
Compound (top) slideCan be set at an angle for tapers and chamfers
Tool postHolds the cutting tool
Leadscrew and feed shaftDrive automatic feed and thread cutting

Lathe dangers

The lathe can catch clothing, hair, gloves or rags and pull a person into the turning work within a second. Flying swarf (chips) is sharp and hot. A chuck key left in the chuck can be thrown out at high speed.

Safety rules

  • Only operate a lathe if trained and authorised.
  • Wear safety glasses, close-fitting overalls with sleeves rolled or buttoned, and safety boots.
  • Tie back long hair; remove rings, watches and chains.
  • Do not wear gloves near the rotating chuck.
  • Never leave the chuck key in the chuck. Make it a habit to remove it immediately.
  • Keep guards in place and know where the emergency stop is.
  • Never touch, measure or clean the work while it is turning.
  • Remove swarf with a brush or hook, never with your hands, and only when the machine is stopped.
  • Never leave a running lathe unattended.

lessons.title: Setting up the work and tools
lessons.html:
Preparing to turn

Read the drawing

Before starting, study the drawing or sample part. Note the material, dimensions, tolerances, chamfers and surface finish. Plan the order of operations, for example: face, centre drill, turn outside diameter, turn step, chamfer, part off.

Holding the workpiece

  • Use a three-jaw chuck for round bar; it centres automatically.
  • Use a four-jaw chuck for square or irregular shapes, or for accurate centring with a dial indicator.
  • Grip enough of the work in the jaws. Do not let too much stick out unsupported. As a general rule, long work needs support from the tailstock centre.
  • Tighten the chuck firmly using the chuck key in each key hole, then remove the key.
  • Turn the chuck by hand once to check nothing hits the bed, carriage or tool.

Cutting tools

Common tools are high-speed steel (HSS) tool bits and tungsten carbide inserts. Types include right-hand and left-hand turning tools, facing tools, parting-off tools and boring bars.

  • Set the tool point exactly at the centre height of the work. Use the tailstock centre or a height gauge to check. A tool that is too high or too low cuts poorly and can leave a pip when facing.
  • Keep the tool overhang short so it does not vibrate (chatter).
  • Make sure the tool post is tight.

Speeds and feeds

Spindle speed depends on the material, the tool material and the diameter of the work. Larger diameters need lower rpm. Harder materials need lower cutting speeds. Use the speed chart on the lathe or in the workshop. The feed is how far the tool moves for each turn of the work. A coarse feed removes metal fast for roughing; a fine feed gives a better finish.

Coolant

Use cutting fluid as recommended for the material to cool the tool and improve finish. Avoid skin contact for long periods and wash your hands after work.

lessons.title: Turning operations and checking the part
lessons.html:
Basic turning operations

Facing

Facing makes the end of the work flat and square. Feed the tool across the end using the cross-slide, from the outside towards the centre, with the carriage locked.

Centre drilling and drilling

Fit a centre drill in a drill chuck in the tailstock. Use a high speed and feed gently to make a small cone-shaped hole. This guides a larger drill or supports work on a tailstock centre. Clear chips often when drilling deep holes.

Parallel turning

Parallel turning reduces the diameter along a length. Take a roughing cut, then measure. Then take a lighter finishing cut to reach the final size. Use the cross-slide dial to set the depth of cut. Remember that a depth of cut of 0.5 mm reduces the diameter by 1 mm, because metal is removed from both sides of the work.

Step turning and chamfering

Steps are shoulders between two diameters. Turn the larger diameter first, then the smaller. A chamfer removes the sharp edge, often at 45°, using a chamfer tool or the compound slide.

Parting off

Parting off cuts the finished part from the bar. Use a sharp parting tool set exactly at centre height, a low speed, plenty of coolant and steady feed. Keep the tool close to the chuck. Do not try to catch the part as it falls.

Monitoring the cut

  • Listen and watch for chatter, squealing or blue smoking swarf, which mean the speed, feed or tool is wrong.
  • Watch for long stringy swarf that can wrap around the work; stop and clear it safely.
  • Check the tool for wear and replace or sharpen when needed.

Measuring and checking

Stop the lathe before measuring. Use a vernier caliper or micrometer to check diameters and lengths against the drawing. Check finish visually, and deburr sharp edges with a file, with the file handle fitted and your arms clear of the chuck. Record results if a quality sheet is used.

Cleaning up

Isolate the lathe, remove swarf with a brush, wipe slideways and oil them lightly. Return tools and leave the machine ready for the next user.

Key points

  • Never leave the chuck key in the chuck and never wear gloves near the rotating chuck.
  • Set the tool at centre height with short overhang.
  • Larger diameters and harder materials need lower spindle speeds.
  • A 0.5 mm depth of cut reduces the diameter by 1 mm.
  • Stop the lathe before measuring or clearing swarf.
  • Clean and oil the lathe after use.
